title: Session 2: dplyr
text:
What is dplyr

dplyr is a core package of the tidyverse
it supports data wrangling

title: Session 2: dplyr
text:
What is the tidyverse?

the tidyverse is a collection of packages supporting a shared way of doing things, which I’ll call the tidyverse approach
there are 9 core tidyverse packages
there are also numerous other packages that share the tidyverse approach

title: Session 2: dplyr
section: So what is the tidyverse approach?
text:
So what is the tidyverse approach?

the tidyverse approach involves:

piping everything
using tidyverse functions
avoiding dollar-sign notation
insisting on two-dimensional output

title: Session 2: dplyr
text:
Setup for some coming examples

load dplyr:


library(dplyr)


import the NHANES data:


nhanes <- read.csv('nhanes_l.csv')

title: Session 2: dplyr
Session 2: dplyr
text:
Piping everything

using base R, we could view the first few rows of minidata like this:


head(minidata)
#|     seqn ridageyr bpxosy1 bpxodi1
#| 1 130378       43     135      98
#| 2 130379       66     121      84
#| 3 130380       44     111      79
#| 4 130384       43      NA      NA
#| 5 130385       65      NA      NA
#| 6 130386       34     110      72

title: Session 2: dplyr
text:
Piping everything

tidyverse users would tend to always use piping:


minidata |> head()
#|     seqn ridageyr bpxosy1 bpxodi1
#| 1 130378       43     135      98
#| 2 130379       66     121      84
#| 3 130380       44     111      79
#| 4 130384       43      NA      NA
#| 5 130385       65      NA      NA
#| 6 130386       34     110      72

title: Session 2: dplyr
text:
Using tidyverse functions

tidyverse purists would probably use slice_head() from dplyr:


minidata |> slice_head(n = 6)
#|     seqn ridageyr bpxosy1 bpxodi1
#| 1 130378       43     135      98
#| 2 130379       66     121      84
#| 3 130380       44     111      79
#| 4 130384       43      NA      NA
#| 5 130385       65      NA      NA
#| 6 130386       34     110      72

title: Session 2: dplyr
text:
Insisting on two-dimensional output

the tidyverse approach insists on two-dimensional output



More specifically, the tidyverse users prefer a two-dimensional object class known as a tibble.

title: Session 2: dplyr
text:
Insisting on two-dimensional output

for example, to find the mean level of systolic blood pressure using base R:


mean(nhanes$bpxosy1, na.rm = TRUE) 
#| [1] 122.5617


or, using dollar() from my baseverse package:


nhanes |> dollar(bpxosy1) |> mean(na.rm = TRUE)
#| [1] 122.5617

title: Session 2: dplyr
Session 2: dplyr
text:
Why should I use dplyr?

dplyr and the tidyverse are enormously popular
dplyr also includes functions and approaches that people argue to be easier to understand or easier to read than base-R equivalents
in some cases, dplyr or tidyverse functions can be faster than base-R equivalents

title: Session 2: dplyr
section: Why should I not use dplyr?
text:
Why should I not use dplyr?

my opinion: dplyr and tidyverse are bloated, with a lot of functions overall, including functions that reproduce base-R functions or features
my opinion: the tidyverse approach is too strict
my opinion: the introduction of piping to base R makes dplyr and tidyverse feel even more redundant

title: Session 2: dplyr
text:
Why should I learn dplyr?

it’s good to understand at least a little bit of dplyr—even if you don’t plan on using it—because it’s so popular

title: Session 2: dplyr
text:
Setup for some coming examples






Tip


Please focus on following along. I’m including the code for the setup in case you want to reproduce any of the examples on your own later.




define a mini version of the NHANES data:


minidata <- nhanes |>
  slice(1:8) |>
  select(ridageyr, asthma, smoking, bmxht)

Setup for some coming examples

minidata |> slice_head(n = 6)

#| 3       44                No                 No 152.9

filter()

to subset to people with a history of smoking:

title: Session 2: dplyr
text:
mutate()

to convert bmxht to inches:


minidata <- minidata |>
  mutate(height = bmxht * 0.3937008)


minidata now looks like this:


minidata |> slice_head(n = 5)
#|   bmxht   height
#| 1 179.5 70.66929
#| 2 174.2 68.58268
#| 3 152.9 60.19685
#| 4    NA       NA
#| 5    NA       NA

title: Session 2: dplyr
text:
Defining missing values

the replace() strategy for defining missing values from Session 6 of A Slower Introduction to R can be combined with mutate() and piping:


nhanes <- nhanes |> 
  mutate(ltpa_vigorous = replace(pad820, pad820 == 7777 | pad820 == 9999, NA))

title: Session 2: dplyr
text:
Defining missing values

verifying that ltpa_vigorous is NA when pad820 is 7777 or 9999:


nhanes |>
  select(pad820, ltpa_vigorous) |>
  filter(pad820 == 7777 | pad820 == 9999) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)
#|   pad820 ltpa_vigorous
#| 1   9999            NA
#| 2   9999            NA
#| 3   9999            NA
#| 4   9999            NA
#| 5   9999            NA

title: Session 2: dplyr
text:
Defining categorical variables

all of the strategies from Session 7 of A Slower Introduction to R can be combined with mutate() and piping

title: Session 2: dplyr
Session 2: dplyr
text:
Labeling categorical variables

country looks like this:


nhanes |> count(country)
#|   country    n
#| 1     USA 6519
#| 2   Other 1617
#| 3    <NA>   17


whereas dmdborn4 looks like this:


nhanes |> count(dmdborn4)
#|   dmdborn4    n
#| 1        1 6519
#| 2        2 1617
#| 3       NA   17

title: Session 2: dplyr
Session 2: dplyr
text:
Categorizing continuous variables

or, using base_when() from my baseverse package:


nhanes <- nhanes |>
  mutate(cholesterol = base_when(
    'Desirable' = (lbxtc < 200),
    'Borderline high' = (lbxtc >= 200) & (lbxtc < 240),
    'High' = (lbxtc >= 240)
  ))

title: Session 2: dplyr
text:
Categorizing continuous variables

cholesterol looks like this:


nhanes |> count(cholesterol)
#|       cholesterol    n
#| 1       Desirable 3695
#| 2 Borderline high 1397
#| 3            High  625
#| 4            <NA> 2436

title: Session 2: dplyr
text:
Exercise 4

Use piping and mutate() to define a new variable for weight (bmxwt) in pounds. Hint: bmxwt is in kilograms and there are 2.204623 pounds in 1 kilgoram.
Use piping, mutate(), and factor() to define a new variable called sex. This should be a labelled version of the original gender variable (riagendr). Values of 1 are used for males and values of 0 are used for females. Not:, this should end up matching the existing gender variable.

title: Session 2: dplyr
text:
Comparison

a summary of key dplyr functions and their base-R equivalents:




base R
baseverse
dplyr




subset()

filter()


subset(select=)
keep()
select()


transform()

mutate()

title: Session 2: dplyr
text:
Comparison

many key functions in dplyr reproduce base-R functions
that being said, the dplyr equivalents may be faster or offer other improvements
dplyr and tidyverse overall also offer numerous other functions that some find useful or convenient

title: Session 2: dplyr
text:
Comparison

for example, starts_with() can be used in select() to pick variables beginning with a pattern:


nhanes |> select(starts_with('bpxosy'))


a base-R approach would be:


nhanes |> subset(select=grep('^bpxosy',names(nhanes)))


this uses grep(), a powerful base-R function for searching for text strings

title: Session 2: dplyr
section: Should I use dplyr and tidyverse?
text:
Should I use dplyr and tidyverse?

it’s up to you!

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Example: sqrt()

sqrt(64)
#| [1] 8
64 |> sqrt()
#| [1] 8


traditional use of functions: function(argument)
piping: argument |> function()

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Example: sqrt()

sqrt(64)
#| [1] 8
64 |> sqrt()
#| [1] 8


another way to think about this is that piping reverses the phrasing
in the traditional use of functions, we write the verb and then the noun
with piping, we write the noun and then the verb

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Why would I do this?

I’ll share illustrative examples, highlighting 3 reasons why piping can be useful
I’ll explain the details later
for now, focus on what’s different in the piping examples

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Setup for some coming examples






Tip


Please focus on following along. I’m including the code for the setup in case you want to reproduce any of the examples on your own later.




load some packages:


library(ggplot2) # for ggplot()
library(baseverse) # for base_when()


import the NHANES data:


nhanes <- read.csv('nhanes_l.csv')

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Example: a ggplot scatterplot

ggplot(data = nhanes, mapping = aes(x = bpxodi1, y = bpxosy1)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = 'Diastolic (mmHg)', y = 'Systolic (mmHg)')

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Example: a ggplot scatterplot

with piping, I could instead write this:


nhanes |> ggplot(aes(x = bmxht, y = bmxwt)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = 'Diastolic (mmHg)', y = 'Systolic (mmHg)')


notice that this allows me to omit the data argument in ggplot()

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Example: cholesterol

from A Slower Introduction to R:


nhanes$cholesterol <- base_when(
  'Desirable' = (nhanes$lbxtc < 200),
  'Borderline high' = (nhanes$lbxtc >= 200) & (nhanes$lbxtc < 240),
  'High' = (nhanes$lbxtc >= 240)
)

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Example: cholesterol

with piping, I could instead write this:


nhanes <- nhanes |>
  transform(cholesterol = base_when(
    'Desirable' = (lbxtc < 200),
    'Borderline high' = (lbxtc >= 200) & (lbxtc < 240),
    'High' = (lbxtc >= 240)
  ))


notice that this allows me to omit dollar-sign notation

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Example: a data snippet

suppose that I want to glance at the data for the subset of people with a history of smoking:


head(subset(
  nhanes,
  smoking == 'History of smoking',
  select = c(hypertension, smoking)
))


this is difficult to read because it nests a long use of subset() within head()

title: Session 1: Piping

text:
In summary

you can use piping to avoid the data argument
you can use piping to avoid dollar-sign notation
you can use piping to avoid nested functions

title: Session 1: Piping
section: Haven’t I seen something like this somewhere else?
text:
Haven’t I seen something like this somewhere else?

possibly, yes!
piping is a core feature of the tidyverse, in packages like dplyr
originally, the tidyverse used the character sequence %>%

title: Session 1: Piping
section: Haven’t I seen something like this somewhere else?
text:
Haven’t I seen something like this somewhere else?

in 2021, base R added support for piping, using the character sequence |>
this sequence is known as the native pipe because it is part of base R



With the introduction of the native pipe, many tidyverse users are transitioning to |>, but it’s still possible to use %>% with tidyverse packages.

title: Session 1: Piping
section: So how do I do this?
text:
So how do I do this?

in general, the pattern is: argument |> function()
more precisely, the typical usage is: first argument of the function |> function()



You can actually use pipe the second or third (or greater) argument, but I won’t show you how to do that today.

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
mean()

without piping:


mean(nhanes$bpxodi1, na.rm = TRUE)
#| [1] 74.97469


with piping:


nhanes$bpxodi1 |> mean(na.rm = TRUE)
#| [1] 74.97469


notice that I’ve kept the na.rm argument in mean()
the phrasing is roughly: “with diastolic blood pressure, take the mean, and ignore missing values when you do so”

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
head()

without piping:


head(nhanes, n = 3)


this shows the first 3 rows of nhanes
with piping:


nhanes |> head(n = 3) 


notice that I’ve kept the n argument in head()

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
head() and dim()

without piping:


dim(head(nhanes, n = 3))


with piping:


nhanes |> 
  head(n = 3) |>
  dim()


this forms a longer pipeline
each pipe adds to the result up to that point

title: Session 1: Piping
Session 1: Piping
text:
Keep writing comments

it is common practice to write long pipelines without any comments 😢







Tip


Keep writing comments!

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Keep writing comments

I suggest writing short pipelines with comments, like this:


# subset to people born outside of the us
nhanes <- nhanes |> subset(country=='Other') 

# define age in months
nhanes <- nhanes |> transform(months=ridageyr*12)

# define height in feet
nhanes <- nhanes |> transform(height_feet=bmxht*0.3937008/12)

what would happen if I didn’t include include minidata <-?

transform() with piping

to convert bmxht to inches:


minidata <- minidata |>
  transform(height = bmxht * 0.3937008)


minidata now looks like this:


minidata |> head()
#|   bmxht new_variable   height
#| 1 179.5            1 70.66929
#| 2 174.2            1 68.58268
#| 3 152.9            1 60.19685
#| 4    NA            1       NA
#| 5    NA            1       NA
#| 6 173.3            1 68.22835

text:
Defining missing values

another option, mentioned in Homework 6 from A Slower Introduction to R, is to use is.na() and object assignment
that strategy can be combined with within() and piping:


nhanes <- nhanes |> within({
  ltpa_vigorous <- pad820
  is.na(ltpa_vigorous) <- pad820 == 7777 | pad820 == 9999
})

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Defining missing values

ltpa_vigorous looks like this:


nhanes$ltpa_vigorous |> summary()
#|    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
#|    1.00   30.00   45.00   60.44   60.00  900.00    4480


whereas pad820 looks like this:


nhanes$pad820 |> summary()
#|    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
#|    1.00   30.00   45.00   97.57   60.00 9999.00    4466

Labeling categorical variables

country looks like this:


nhanes$country |> table(useNA='always')
#| 
#|   USA Other  <NA> 
#|  6519  1617    17


whereas dmdborn4 looks like this:


nhanes$dmdborn4 |> table(useNA='always')
#| 
#|    1    2 <NA> 
#| 6519 1617   17

text:
Categorizing continuous variables

or, using base_when() from my baseverse package:


nhanes <- nhanes |>
  transform(cholesterol = base_when(
    'Desirable' = (lbxtc < 200),
    'Borderline high' = (lbxtc >= 200) & (lbxtc < 240),
    'High' = (lbxtc >= 240)
  ))

text:
Exercise 4

Use piping and transform() to define a new variable for weight (bmxwt) in pounds. Hint: bmxwt is in kilograms and there are 2.204623 pounds in 1 kilgoram.
Use piping, transform(), and factor() to define a new variable called sex. This should be a labelled version of the original gender variable (riagendr). Values of 1 are used for males and values of 0 are used for females. Not:, this should end up matching the existing gender variable.

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Should I always use piping?

it’s up to you!
piping can be fun and satisfying
as we’ll discuss next week, tidyverse purists tend to try to pipe everything
I am, in general, supportive of having options…
